entities.summary:
Jean-Michel Beysser (1753–1794) was a French Revolutionary general who fought for the Republic in the early 1790s before falling to the Terror’s suspicion of commanders. Like many officers who accepted the Revolution, he rose quickly as aristocratic emigration emptied the old officer corps and volunteer battalions needed leaders.

Revolutionary generals navigated dual dangers: defeat at the front and political denunciation at home. Beysser’s execution in 1794 places him among the soldiers purged when the Committee of Public Safety equated setbacks or moderation with treason.

He illustrates the lethal precariousness of military authority under the Jacobin war republic—promotion by merit, death by faction.
